subject: Re: questions (new user) re: convergence failure & cluster size

messages.subject: Re: questions (new user) re: convergence failure & cluster size
parts:
Hi Jay,

I'll reply to the list, so that my reply is in the archives for others wondering
about the same issues.

Firstly, I did you search, rather than browse the list archives?
(Click on "Search the archives" at
http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/lists/distance-sampling.html)
I ask because I tried typing in "convergence" to the search box and found two
messages that address much of your first question (messages 158 and 548) and
typed in "size bias" to find at least one that addresses your second (message
27).

Have a look at those messages, and then the following.

The first thing you should do, after a detailed exploratory examination of your
data, is think about truncation. Look under "Truncation" in the index of
Introduction to Distance Sampling for more on this. Also look under "Analysis,
guidelines" in the book or online help for suggestions about how to approach an
analysis.

If, once you've truncated, you get convergence warnings, you should look and see
which model they occur for. If you're using sequential selection of adjustment
terms (the default) and it occurs for a model with lots of adjustment terms and
that model is subsequently not selected as it has a higher AIC than one with
fewer adjustments, then there's probably nothing to worry about. I think I
showed an example of this in either message 158 or 548. In some rare cases, you
can get convergence problems even for models with few adjustments, particularly
for the hazard rate key function and even more so when you're using covariates
(the MCDS analysis engine). In this case, you may need to experiment with
setting starting values and/or putting bounds on the parameters. This is
particularly so for the shape parameter of the hazard rate function (usually
labelled A(2) in the results) for which an upper bound can sometimes need to be
set for data with a "spike" at zero distance. (In this case, if the "spike" is
due to rounding of distances to zero or to movement of animals onto the line
then converting the data into intervals is a more effective and defensible
solution.)

Regarding the size bias warning; we normally expect large clusters of animals to
be easier to detect than small clusters at large distances, so a regression of
cluster size against distance from the line has a positive slope. For reasons
outlined in the book (look in the index under "size biased sampling"), the
default regression in Distance is actually log(cluster size) against detection
probability, which we expect to have a negative slope.

In some cases, the estimated slope can go the other way - i.e., the regression
of log(cluster size) against detection probability has a positive slope. One
obvious reason for this is that the slope is an estimate, subject to sampling
error, so it could just be chance. Another is that the true slope really is
positive: that you really are more likely to record smaller clusters at greater
distances from the line (and so lower probability of detection). This can occur
if you underestimate cluster size at these larger distances (can't see the whole
cluster). The regression still works fine though -- the estimated intercept at
zero distance is still an unbiased estimate of average cluster size in the
population.

Hope this helps,

- Len
